title: Direct Instruction Is the American Default
author: Michael Pershan
summary: Michael Pershan responds to Matt Yglesias and Emily Hanford, who suggest that American schools abandoned direct instruction for inquiry. He starts from the 1995 and 1999 TIMSS video studies of Grade 8 math lessons, which showed teachers explaining, assigning practice, and changing little, and argues the pattern still holds. Teachers he consulted, plus Larry Cuban's research, say teacher explanation remains the dominant mode even though the rhetoric of inquiry is everywhere, as when the JUMP Math curriculum calls itself guided discovery. Progressive curricula such as Illustrative Mathematics are often bent back into the default by teachers who skip the teacher notes and add explanation and routine practice. Pershan's central claim is that this is not an ideological fight: the research-backed, fussy version of direct instruction, with choral response, cold-calling, and bursts of worked examples, is simply harder to teach than the easy default. Anyone who wants teachers to teach more ambitiously needs a plan for the added work, not just a better argument.
points: The TIMSS video studies and Larry Cuban's work suggest American teaching has changed little in thirty years, and mostly consists of explanation followed by practice.
Inquiry is popular as rhetoric even among direct instruction advocates, which makes the profession look more progressive than it is.
Curriculum is easily subverted, since teachers often skip the teacher notes and convert problem-based materials into mediocre direct instruction.
Effective direct instruction is demanding because it involves many moving parts, so teachers drift toward the easiest version of the job.
Pershan reframes the reform problem as one of effort and support rather than ideas, which implies leaders must make better teaching easier to do.
quotes: Despite massive efforts to improve teaching in the United States, and despite perceptions by many that teaching was, in fact, improving, we found no evidence that anything had changed between 1995 and 1999.
Progressive ideas are widespread. Most people talk the talk. But walk into 100 random classrooms this morning and my guess is you will see teacher explanation as the dominant teaching mechanism.
Why is the paradigmatic direct instruction resource describing itself as “guided discovery”? Simple: everyone in education uses the rhetoric of inquiry.
In short, teachers are often assimilating the curriculum to the default pedagogy. They are transforming IM into mediocre direct instruction.
American teachers excel at taking just a bit of some new idea, while basically keeping everything the same.
Effective direct instruction—the kind that advocates are advocating for—is not easy to teach. I called it “fussy” for a reason.
The easiest way to teach is to give kids something they know how to do, then give them time to do it.
If anyone want teachers to teach differently, to be more ambitious, they have to expect for it to be harder. You need a plan for getting teachers not just to agree with you, but to do more work.
